title: Musculoskeletal and Integumentary Terminology

sections.learningObjectives:
- Define musculoskeletal and integumentary word parts (roots, prefixes, and suffixes).
- Build and decode medical terms for the muscular, skeletal, and integumentary systems.
- Recognize common musculoskeletal and integumentary conditions and procedures by their terminology.
- Apply safe, scope-appropriate responses to clinical situations involving these systems.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

The word part my/o is like a label that says 'this word is about muscles.' Once you know it, you can guess that any word starting with 'my' is talking about muscle.

### Question 2

Oste/o is the 'bone' label, like a name tag that says bone. Words with 'oste' in them are about the skeleton.

### Question 3

Arthr/o is the 'joint' label. Words like arthritis are just saying 'the joint is swollen or sore.'

### Question 4

Dermat/o is the 'skin' label — a dermatologist is simply a 'skin doctor.'

### Question 5

Cartilage is the smooth, rubbery cushion in joints. Chondr/o is the label that means 'cartilage.'

### Question 6

A tendon is the strong cord that connects muscle to bone. Tendin/o is its label, so tendinitis is a sore tendon.

### Question 7

Crani/o is the 'skull' label, like the helmet of bone that protects your brain.

### Question 8

Cost/o is the 'rib' label. 'Intercostal' simply means 'between the ribs.'

### Question 9

Vertebrae are the stacked building blocks of your spine. Spondyl/o is one label for these spine bones.

### Question 10

Onych/o is the 'nail' label — fingernails and toenails.

### Question 11

Trich/o is the 'hair' label, like the fuzz on your head and body.

### Question 12

Melanin is the dark pigment that gives skin its color. Melan/o is the label for that dark pigment.

### Question 13

Erythr/o is the 'red' label. Erythema is just redness of the skin.

### Question 14

Hidr/o is the 'sweat' label. Hyperhidrosis is just 'too much sweat.'

### Question 15

Sebum is the natural oil your skin makes. Seb/o is its label, so seborrhea means too much oil.

### Question 16

A bursa is like a tiny water balloon that cushions a joint. Burs/o is its label, so bursitis is a sore cushion.

### Question 17

Cutane/o is another 'skin' label, like dermat/o. Subcutaneous means 'under the skin.'

### Question 18

Striated muscle is the striped muscle you control to move. Rhabdomy/o is its label.

### Question 19

Peri- is like a wrapper: it means 'around.' The periosteum wraps around the bone like cling film.

### Question 20

Sub- means 'under,' like a submarine goes under water. Subcutaneous is 'under the skin.'

### Question 21

Intra- means 'inside.' An intramuscular shot goes inside the muscle.

### Question 22

Endo- means 'inside.' The endosteum is the lining on the inside of a bone, while the periosteum wraps the outside.

### Question 23

Dys- means something is going wrong or is hard. Dystrophy means tissue is developing badly.

### Question 24

Hyper- means 'too much' or 'extra.' Hypertrophy is when a muscle gets bigger than usual.

### Question 25

Hypo- means 'too little.' Hypotonia is when muscles are too floppy or weak.

### Question 26

A- means 'without.' Atrophy is when a muscle shrinks from not being used, like a plant that wilts without water.

### Question 27

-dynia is another 'ouch' ending, a twin of -algia. Osteodynia means a bone ache.

### Question 28

-osis is the 'condition' ending. Osteoporosis just means 'a condition of holes in the bone.'

### Question 29

-rrhexis is the 'burst' ending. Myorrhexis means a muscle tore apart.

### Question 30

Osteoclasts are the 'bone breakers' that clear away old bone; osteoblasts are the 'bone builders.'

### Question 31

Osteoblasts are the young 'bone builders'; they grow up into osteocytes, the settled bone cells.

### Question 32

Osteocytes are the grown-up bone cells that finished building and now maintain the bone.

### Question 33

Myalgia = 'muscle' + 'ouch.' It is the word for sore, aching muscles.

### Question 34

Osteomalacia = 'bone' + 'getting soft.' The bones lose strength and become bendy.

### Question 35

Arthroplasty = 'joint' + 'fix.' It is surgery to repair a joint, often by replacing it.

### Question 36

Dermatitis = 'skin' + 'swollen and sore.' It is the general word for irritated skin.

### Question 37

Onychomycosis = 'nail' + 'fungus' + 'condition' — a fungal nail infection, like athlete's foot of the nail.

### Question 38

Rhabdomyolysis = 'muscle' + 'breaking apart.' Damaged muscle cells spill their contents into the blood.

### Question 39

Osteoporosis = 'bone' + 'full of holes.' Bones become fragile and break more easily.

### Question 40

Tendinitis = 'tendon' + 'swollen and sore.' It is an overuse injury of the cord that pulls a muscle.

### Question 41

Osteomyelitis = 'bone' + 'marrow' + 'infection.' It is a serious infection inside a bone.

### Question 42

Arthrocentesis = 'joint' + 'drain with a needle.' It removes fluid to relieve swelling or test for disease.

### Question 43

Osteoarthritis is like the tread on a tire wearing down over years — the cushion in a joint slowly thins.

### Question 44

Rheumatoid arthritis is when the body's own defense system mistakenly attacks the joints on both sides of the body.

### Question 45

Osteoporosis makes bones like a sponge with too many holes, so they snap more easily.

### Question 46

A sprain hurts the strong bands that hold bones together (ligaments); a strain hurts the muscles or cords that move you.

### Question 47

An open fracture is when a broken bone pokes out or the skin is broken over it — you can 'see' the break.

### Question 48

A nerve gets squeezed in a narrow 'tunnel' in your wrist, making the hand feel tingly or numb.

### Question 49

Tendinitis is a sore cord; bursitis is a sore cushion. Both hurt near a joint but involve different parts.

### Question 50

Gout is like tiny sharp crystals forming in a joint, causing sudden, intense pain.

### Question 51

In myasthenia gravis, the messages between nerves and muscles get blocked, so muscles tire out quickly.

### Question 52

Muscular dystrophy is a family of conditions passed down in genes that make muscles get weaker over time.

### Question 53

Melanoma is the 'serious' skin cancer that starts in pigment cells and can travel to other parts of the body.

### Question 54

Basal cell carcinoma is the 'everyday' skin cancer — very common, usually easy to treat when caught early.

### Question 55

In psoriasis, skin cells pile up too fast, making dry, scaly patches — like a stack of plates that keeps growing.

### Question 56

Eczema makes skin feel itchy and look red and dry, like a rash that keeps coming back.

### Question 57

In vitiligo, the cells that make skin color stop working in spots, leaving pale patches.

### Question 58

Alopecia is the doctor's word for hair falling out or thinning.

### Question 59

Arthroscopy is like sending a tiny camera into a joint to look around without a big cut.

### Question 60

A total knee or hip replacement is an arthroplasty — 'fixing' the joint by putting in new parts.

### Question 61

ORIF means a surgeon puts a broken bone back in place and holds it together with metal screws and plates.

### Question 62

A biopsy is taking a tiny piece of skin to look at under a microscope and see if it is healthy or not.

### Question 63

Debridement is like clearing dead weeds out of a garden so healthy plants can grow.

### Question 64

I&D is opening a 'pocket of pus' like a boil to let it drain out so it can heal.

### Question 65

Cryosurgery freezes off a wart or spot, like how frost damages a plant so it falls away.

### Question 66

A DEXA scan checks how strong and solid your bones are, like testing whether a beam is sturdy.

### Question 67

An EMG listens to the tiny electrical signals muscles make when they move, to see if the muscles and nerves are working.

### Question 68

If a wound looks angry — red, hot, swollen, and oozing — the assistant tells the doctor right away, because it might be infected.

### Question 69

If a cast squeezes too tight, the arm can't get enough blood — the assistant must tell the doctor right away, like a smoke alarm going off.

### Question 70

Measuring a wound is like recording the size of a puddle each day — writing down the numbers lets the doctor see if it is shrinking or growing.
